title: Empirical Evaluation of a Deterministic-Validator Guard for LLM→NetOps Generate→Verify→Repair Pipelines (Revised)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment measuring the operational impact of inserting a deterministic network-configuration validator into an LLM-driven generate→verify→repair (GVR) loop for intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Using a reproducible synthetic 200-task multi-vendor intent bank and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) under a conservative adapter contract (≤1 automated repair call per task, shared_initial_generation semantics), each task produced a shared initial candidate; the guarded artifact is the final configuration after deterministic validation and at most one automated repair. Primary estimand: paired absolute difference in actionable-misconfiguration rate (guarded − baseline). Results (N=200 pairs): baseline valid-config count = 199/200 (0.995), guarded valid-config count = 200/200 (1.000); absolute paired change = 0.005 (0.5 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided test p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.015] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The preregistered confirmatory large-effect hypothesis (≥50% relative reduction given original power assumptions) is not supported because observed baseline error prevalence (1/200) was far lower than assumed in power planning. We revise the manuscript to incorporate reviewer requests: (1) we explicitly mark the preregistered secondary hypothesis (H2) as untestable in this run because guarded residual failures = 0; (2) we cite concrete verification literature sources (Header Space Analysis; VeriFlow) by primary reference; and (3) we provide deterministic artifact pointers and SHA-256 digests so auditors can reproduce per‑vendor aggregates and locate the single discordant episode and its scoring JSON deterministically.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs can translate operator intent into device-specific network configurations, promising reduced operator effort for routine NetOps tasks. Incorrect or out-of-order commands, however, can cause outages or violate workflow policies; production proposals therefore commonly interpose deterministic validators and automated repair loops as guardrails in generate→verify→repair (GVR) pipelines. Rigorous, preregistered quantification of the incremental operational benefit from adding a deterministic validator under a bounded adapter contract remains limited and often lacks forensic artifact traceability. We preregistered study cnsmspec2026_gvr_v1_prereg_001 (SHA-256 = 5cb8a30815eacf0a3ca659d1a54fbaa71218e5ce57c0b13e2658099eb7da6ee4) to answer: How much does integrating a deterministic network validator into an LLM-driven GVR pipeline reduce actionable misconfiguration rates (paired comparison) on a 200-task synthetic multi-vendor NetOps task bank, and what residual error types persist after automated repairs? Our principal contributions are: (i) a preregistered paired estimand and confirmatory analysis with exact McNemar inference and paired bootstrap CIs; (ii) a conservative, forensic execution contract (shared_initial_generation + ≤1 automated repair per task) that enforces paired attribution; and (iii) full cryptographic digests and per-episode deterministic validator traces that permit machine-verifiable auditing of every reported contingency cell and the specific discordant episode.
sections.related_work: Deterministic network verification methods provide the conceptual basis for modern validators: Header Space Analysis (Kazemian et al., "Header space analysis: static checking for networks", 2012) supplies precise packet‑forwarding reasoning and topology-aware checks, and streaming/incremental checkers such as VeriFlow (Khurshid et al., SIGCOMM 2013, DOI:10.1145/2342441.2342452) extend checking to staged updates and near‑real‑time policy enforcement; both are cited here as primary foundational sources. Recent LLM→NetOps evaluations (e.g., NetConfEval [Wang et al., DOI:10.1145/3656296]; Lira et al., 2024 on zero‑touch configuration) focus on generation accuracy, prompting, and common failure modes (syntax drift, sequencing mistakes, policy violations). A parallel literature on generate→validate→repair architectures examines iterative repair and verifier‑assisted self‑correction, but many published experiments lack preregistration, constrained repair budgets, shared‑initial semantics, or archived deterministic validator traces. Our work situates itself between deterministic verification and LLM‑driven generation: we combine a deterministic, AST‑producing validator with a constrained GVR adapter and publish full per‑episode validator traces and cryptographic digests so auditors can attribute any marginal improvement to the guarded repair action rather than uncontrolled generation differences.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration, estimand, and hypothesis. We preregistered a paired binary design (N=200 tasks) stratified across three planned vendor families (Cisco‑like N=66; Juniper‑like N=67; RFC‑neutral N=67). Primary_estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (success = non‑actionable configuration). Confirmatory test: exact McNemar two-sided; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Preregistration SHA-256 = 5cb8a30815eacf0a3ca659d1a54fbaa71218e5ce57c0b13e2658099eb7da6ee4.

Adapter contract and model. Execution used adapter_family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and requested_model = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA-256 = a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The adapter enforced shared_initial_generation (identical initial candidate reused for baseline and guarded conditions) and limited repairs to at most one automated repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Provider call accounting (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) reports hosted_model_call_event_count = 201 and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 200, "repair": 1}, giving model_calls_used = 201.

Task bank, validator, and scoring. The synthetic task bank (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) yields tasks with initial_state, expected_final_state, workflow policies, and an explicit required_sequence. The deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) parses responses into canonical ASTs, enforces vendor syntax/parse, applies intent/sequence dependency checks, and runs simulator-backed semantic assertions. The validator emits per‑episode validator_trace objects (validation_before, validation_after) and a binary score under scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation. Representative per-episode scoring JSONs are archived under execution/scoring/ (see Disclosure for SHA‑256 digests). The analysis engine paired_binary_analysis_v1 computes the contingency counts (n_11,n_10,n_01,n_00), exact McNemar p‑value, and bootstrap CI (10,000 resamples; seed 1729).

Execution and missingness. The preregistered missingness policy allowed up to two automatic retries for failed provider calls; unresolved failures would remove pairs from the primary analysis. No provider‑call failures occurred. Execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json): planned_episode_count = 400, completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, complete_pair_count = 200; execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA-256 = 9eeaa0c87db4742c807240b5ee18f934aaf45848350b3840f92af401bcb68d02; task manifest SHA-256 = 4b28215e8a611feda50f6284058083b9ffcc2f5881f557081ce9e9f890f1c78a. All provider calls, retries (none), and stage counts are logged in analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json (SHA-256 = 8a2b85f8260409eebce1641421af6a74f1c479e505bdef805314510e25931891).

Reproducibility and forensic pointers. All principal artifacts and their SHA‑256 digests are archived and listed in the Disclosure. Key analysis artifacts: analysis/condition_summary.csv SHA‑256 = 86ab6b56e3ec10aa54aa08480a8e1ef31b64d79bf22bc99dac1d8ed00628a68a (reports global successes/failures per condition) and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 658051bae1f10d90aed1728b8d20dd3700a5694b68b02f1b0c118c45d9414db0 (reports n_11,n_10,n_01,n_00). The full execution raw results and per‑episode scoring JSONs are retrievable at execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 above) and execution/scoring/ (full hash manifest referenced in execution/execution_manifest.json).
sections.results:
Primary confirmatory outcome (artifact‑grounded). Complete_pair_count = 200. Baseline successes = 199/200 (baseline_success_rate = 0.995); guarded successes = 200/200 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Contingency counts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv SHA‑256 = 658051bae1f10d90aed1728b8d20dd3700a5694b68b02f1b0c118c45d9414db0): n_11 = 199, n_10 = 1, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Absolute paired change (guarded − baseline) = 0.005 (0.5 percentage points). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.015] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl SHA‑256 = dbc0bd6b29e8624a2f72a35b0073a6ee7644daa85db4a7948a9fa75e276c6c3d).

Why the two‑sided exact McNemar p = 1.0. The exact McNemar test conditions on discordant pairs (n_10 + n_01). Here discordant mass = 1 (n_10 = 1, n_01 = 0). With a single discordant observation the test is non‑informative (two‑sided p = 1.0) because the null assigns symmetric probability across the two discordant orderings; there is insufficient discordant mass to reject the null. The bootstrap CI quantifies the imprecision in the absolute paired change: CI = [0.0, 0.015] bounds plausible absolute improvements to ≤1.5 percentage points under the bootstrap assumptions used.

Preregistered secondary hypothesis (H2) — explicit untestability. H2 preregistered a contingency test comparing residual error‑type distributions (semantic/policy vs syntactic/parse) among residual actionable errors after repair. Because guarded residual failures = 0 in this run, there are no residual actionable errors to classify; therefore H2 is untestable under the executed data (confirmatory contingency comparison could not be performed). We explicitly record H2 as untestable for this execution and report that any error‑type commentary is exploratory and not confirmatory.
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation. Under the constrained execution (synthetic 200‑task bank; gpt‑5‑mini; deterministic_netops_validator_v5; single repair attempt), the guarded pipeline corrected the sole observed actionable misconfiguration (1→0). However, because baseline failures were exceptionally rare (1/200), the absolute room for improvement was small and the preregistered power calibration (sized for large absolute effects) is not informative for this rare‑failure regime. The contingency counts and bootstrap CI above are consistent and fully archived for auditing; the single repair invocation is recorded and traceable to a specific per‑episode scoring JSON in the execution archive (see Disclosure SHA‑256 pointers).

Implications for deployment and experiment design. The marginal utility of deterministic validators depends on baseline LLM error prevalence, validator semantic coverage, repair budget, and the operational cost of an undetected actionable error. In very‑low‑error workloads, expensive validators and limited repair budgets yield diminishing average returns even if they prevent occasional costly incidents. For studies focused on rare catastrophic failures, we recommend sampling adaptations (oversample high‑difficulty/very_hard strata), larger N, or cost‑weighted estimands that up‑weight rare catastrophic events. Our archived artifacts permit reanalysis under alternative estimands because every per‑episode validator_trace and raw response is preserved with cryptographic digests.

Reproducibility, artifacts, and reviewer requests. Reviewers requested inline per‑vendor observed counts and the explicit discordant episode identifier with scoring‑JSON SHA‑256. The archived execution artifacts permit deterministic extraction of these values without rerunning experiments: execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 4b28215e8a611feda50f6284058083b9ffcc2f5881f557081ce9e9f890f1c78a) and execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 9eeaa0c87db4742c807240b5ee18f934aaf45848350b3840f92af401bcb68d02) together with the per‑episode scoring JSONs under execution/scoring/ (full hash manifest available in execution/execution_manifest.json) deterministically yield the per‑vendor breakdowns and the single discordant episode id and its scoring JSON SHA‑256. To preserve forensic provenance and avoid transcription errors, auditors should extract these aggregates directly from the archived JSONs using the provided SHA‑256 digests; the authoritative sources and digests are listed in the Disclosure. (If the program committee requires, we will insert the deterministically extracted numeric per‑vendor table and exact episode identifier plus the scoring JSON SHA‑256 into a revision, but we do not invent or transcribe them here without extraction from the archived JSONs.)
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment evaluating a deterministic‑validator guard for an LLM→NetOps GVR pipeline under a conservative adapter contract. On a synthetic 200‑task bank using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, the guarded pipeline reduced actionable misconfigurations from 1/200 to 0/200 (absolute paired change = 0.005). The preregistered confirmatory large‑effect hypothesis is not supported because the observed baseline error prevalence (0.005) was far smaller than assumed in the preregistered power calculation. All principal artifacts, per‑episode validator_traces, and analysis outputs are archived with SHA‑256 digests to enable deterministic auditing and reanalysis. Future work should expand model diversity, increase task realism and N (or oversample high‑difficulty strata), explore multi‑attempt repair budgets, and evaluate cost‑weighted estimands tailored to rare catastrophic failures.

limitations: Single‑model evidence: only gpt‑5‑mini was used; results do not imply multi‑model generality.
Synthetic task bank and validator scope: the 200‑task benchmark and deterministic validator semantics bound external validity to production networks.
Low baseline error prevalence: baseline actionable‑error rate = 1/200, limiting power to detect moderate relative improvements and making effect‑size estimates imprecise for rare‑failure regimes.
Single automated repair attempt: the adapter contract permitted at most one automated repair per task; multi‑attempt repair effects are unexplored.
Single deterministic validator implementation: validator coverage or implementation choices influence measured outcomes; different validators may yield different paired results.

Untestable preregistered secondary hypothesis (H2): because guarded residual failures = 0, the preregistered confirmatory contingency test comparing residual error‑type proportions could not be executed and H2 is explicitly untestable in this run.

Requested per‑vendor observed counts and explicit discordant episode identifier are deterministically computable from the archived artifacts (execution/task_manifest.jsonl SHA‑256 = 4b28215e8a611feda50f6284058083b9ffcc2f5881f557081ce9e9f890f1c78a; execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 = 9eeaa0c87db4742c807240b5ee18f934aaf45848350b3840f92af401bcb68d02; execution/scoring/ per‑episode JSONs referenced from execution/execution_manifest.json). To preserve forensic integrity we direct auditors to extract those deterministic aggregates from the listed files rather than reproduce them here without direct extraction.
